title: How AI Facial Recognition Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how AI facial recognition works: neural nets since around 2007 improved machine learning, facial geometry measurement and normalization, similarity scores rather than definitive matches, and beneficial uses (tagging, Thorn anti-trafficking, dating apps, finding people who cannot identify themselves). They then cover harms: government and police surveillance, China's CCTV targeting of ethnic minorities, bans in San Francisco, Oakland, Berkeley and Somerville, Maine, the NYPD using a Woody Harrelson lookalike, racial accuracy disparities, Fourth Amendment questions, Amazon Rekognition, and Clearview AI scraping social media. The episode ends with listener mail thanking fans for gifts.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour announcement
segments.summary: Josh announces spring tour dates in Vancouver and Portland, then the hosts chat about old movies (Short Circuit, War Games) and early computer games before turning to facial recognition.

segments.title: History and why facial recognition improved
segments.summary: The hosts note facial recognition dates to the 1950s and a 2002 Super Bowl test went poorly. Neural nets around 2007 let machines learn faces from example images. Facebook's photo volume and cheaper tools expanded use.

segments.title: Amazon Rekognition and wide availability
segments.summary: Amazon offers a cheap facial recognition service called Rekognition that law enforcement and other platforms can subscribe to, making the technology ubiquitous. Josh offers a soapbox warning about privacy, citing Woodrow Hartzog's view that surveillance could become irreversible.

segments.title: How the process works: facial geometry and normalization
segments.summary: The system measures facial geometry, such as distances between features, then normalizes the face to a front-facing view, compares it to databases of mostly face-on photos, and uses nodal points. The hosts discuss 2D versus 3D (Apple's Face ID) and sunglasses blocking phone unlocking.

segments.title: Similarity scores, not certainty
segments.summary: The software outputs a probabilistic similarity score rather than a definitive match. The user sets the confidence threshold, and Amazon's default recommended threshold is discussed as creepy.

segments.title: Beneficial uses of facial recognition
segments.summary: Beneficial uses include tagging photos, Thorn's work scanning missing children's photos against exploitation material and rescuing about a hundred kids, dating apps, Taylor Swift's security team scanning audiences for known harassers, and police identifying people who cannot identify themselves, such as the amnesia case of Benjamin Kyle.

segments.title: Surveillance abuses, bans, and wrongful arrest risks
segments.summary: Harmful uses include China's CCTV systems targeting ethnic minorities and religious groups. San Francisco, Oakland, Berkeley and Somerville, Maine have banned law enforcement use. The NYPD used a Woody Harrelson lookalike to match a beer thief at a CVS. The Georgetown study Garbage In, Garbage Out is cited. The FBI gets about fifty thousand search requests a month. Using driver's license databases puts everyone in a perpetual lineup.

segments.title: Racial bias, Amazon's dispute, and legal questions
segments.summary: An MIT Media Lab 2018 study found higher misidentification rates for darker-skinned women and men, which the hosts attribute to unrepresentative training data. Amazon disputed this by distinguishing facial analysis from facial recognition. The hosts discuss Fourth Amendment questions, checkpoint precedent, and Carpenter v. United States.

segments.title: Clearview AI and the broader surveillance concern
segments.summary: The New York Times exposed Clearview AI, which scrapes social media to build a database of about three billion photos sold to law enforcement. The hosts discuss ring doorbells, smart devices, and the danger of a surveillance society.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for gifts and letters, including socks, t-shirts, portraits, books, and food, and invite emails to the show address.
